items.canonical_answer: Money is anything that people generally accept as payment for goods and services and for settling debts; its forms include coins, notes and bank deposits.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state general acceptance as payment for goods, services and debts, and may name its forms such as coins, notes and bank deposits.

items.canonical_answer: Durability: money survives being passed from hand to hand, so it lasts as a means of payment. Divisibility: money splits into small units, so a buyer can pay exactly N$15 for a small purchase rather than swap a whole animal.
marking_guidance: Features: one mark per characteristic named from the list - acceptability, durability, portability, divisibility, uniformity, scarcity - with credit for what the quality means.
Elements: credit any two characteristics; a function of money such as medium of exchange, unit of account or store of value comes from the other list and is not a characteristic.

items.prompt: At a craft market in Katutura a wood-carver sells a carving for N$80 and, the same afternoon, buys a 10 kg bag of maize meal for N$45 in coins and notes. Before the market used money she had to find one trader who both wanted a carving and sold maize. Using the context, explain how money working as a medium of exchange helps this trader, and why trade tends to be quicker with money than with barter.
items.canonical_answer: Before money, the carver needed a double coincidence of wants: one trader who both wanted a carving and sold maize, and finding that trader took time away from carving. With money as a medium of exchange, she can sell the carving to any buyer with N$80 and pay the maize seller N$45 in notes and coins, because both accept money. Each purchase therefore takes one meeting instead of a search, which means trade with money tends to be quicker and wider than barter.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures - the N$80 carving and the N$45 bag of maize meal - and the before-money situation must be used.
Reasoning: the link from money as a medium of exchange to quicker trade must be made, because removing the double coincidence of wants is the mechanism.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must state what the medium of exchange does for the trader - one meeting per purchase instead of one search.

items.prompt: Suppose sellers across an economy began to doubt the notes and coins they were paid in, and started to demand goods in direct barter instead. Discuss the likely consequences for consumers, producers and the government of an economy where money stops being accepted.
items.canonical_answer: If sellers refuse money and demand goods, exchange falls back on barter. Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each trader must find a partner who wants what is offered and offers what is wanted. This causes each purchase to take longer, so fewer trades happen. Consumers spend more time searching and get less variety. Producers sell less of their output, so they narrow what they make to what they can swap; specialisation and output fall, and workers in specialised firms face less secure jobs. The government finds taxes harder to collect and salaries harder to pay, because neither is easily settled in goods. The damage is likely to be greatest for specialised producers and smallest where people already swap a few staple goods face to face, and how far output falls depends on how quickly trust in the currency returns.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - sellers demanding goods instead of money - must be named.
Mechanism: the chain through the double coincidence of wants must be spelled out, because slower matching is what causes the fall in trade.
Consequence: the results must land on named parties - consumers, producers, workers, the government.
For whom: each consequence must be attributed to the consumer, worker, firm, government or economy it lands on.

items.canonical_answer: A commercial bank is a financial institution that accepts deposits from households and firms, lends the pooled funds to borrowers, and moves payments between accounts.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning must cover taking deposits from the public and lending the pooled funds, with payment services as a creditable third element.

items.prompt: Explain why commercial banks matter to a producer such as Kaoko Juice of Oshakati and to the consumers who buy its juice.
items.canonical_answer: Kaoko Juice pays for fruit, bottles and wages before its juice sells, and a bank loan bridges that gap. The bank can make the loan because it pools many small deposits into a sum no single saver could lend. The firm's deposit account keeps its takings safe, and transfers pay distant suppliers without cash travelling. Consumers gain because their savings are kept safe, their payments travel over distance, and the loans that reach producers help keep goods on the shelves.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose - bridging the gap between paying costs and receiving revenue - must be stated, because that is why producers borrow.
Development: each reason must be linked to the party it helps, not left as a list of bank services.

items.prompt: A news extract reports: "This month the government paid salaries to 100 000 civil servants through its account at the Bank of Namibia, which also issued 12 million new N$30 notes this year. The salaries landed in accounts held at commercial banks." Using the extract, explain the roles the central bank and the commercial banks play in these payments.
items.canonical_answer: The extract shows two kinds of bank doing different jobs. The central bank, the Bank of Namibia, issued the 12 million N$30 notes and holds the government's account, so it settles the government's side of the salaries paid to 100 000 civil servants. The commercial banks hold the workers' own accounts, where the salaries land, and provide the payment services the workers draw on. Therefore one salary passes through both: the central bank serves the government, whereas the commercial banks serve households.
marking_guidance: Context: the extract - the 100 000 salaries and the 12 million N$30 notes - must be used to anchor each role.
Reasoning: the link from each role to the party it serves must be made, because who the bank serves is the boundary between them.
Conclusion: therefore the answer names which bank settles the government's side and which serves the households.

items.canonical_answer: Medium of exchange: money passes from buyer to seller in payment, so trade needs no double coincidence of wants. Store of value: money can be kept without spoiling and spent later, so income can be saved; it holds its worth best while prices are fairly steady.

items.prompt: A fisher in Lüderitz earns N$60 000 during the four-month lobster season and nothing in the other eight months. Prices in Namibia are rising by about 4% a year. Explain how money acting as a store of value helps her, and what limits it.
items.canonical_answer: She can keep part of the N$60 000 as notes or bank deposits and spend it through the eight months without income, because money does not spoil the way fish would. Income earned in one season pays for food in another: that is money as a store of value. With prices rising by about 4% a year, each Namibian dollar buys a little less as the months pass. Therefore money stores her income well while prices are fairly steady, and faster price rises would weaken it.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer uses the case - N$60 000 earned in four months and eight months without income, with prices rising about 4% a year.
Reasoning: because money can be kept without spoiling, income can be moved from the season to the quiet months.
Conclusion: therefore money stores value well while prices are fairly steady, which means rising prices limit the function.

items.prompt: Identify two roles of a central bank.
items.canonical_answer: Issuer of notes and coins: it issues the country's currency. Lender of last resort: it lends to commercial banks that face a sudden rush of withdrawals.
marking_guidance: Features: one mark per role named, from what it includes - issuing notes and coins, banker to the government, banker to the commercial banks, lender of last resort, setting the interest rate, managing foreign currency reserves, supervising commercial banks.
A service a commercial bank gives households, such as a savings account or a car loan, is not a central bank role and is not credited.

items.prompt: Explain why a central bank acts as lender of last resort to commercial banks.
items.canonical_answer: A commercial bank lends out most of its deposits and keeps part of them as cash. If many depositors try to withdraw at once, even a sound bank may run short. The central bank can lend it cash quickly, so depositors are paid and panic is less likely to spread to other banks. Because of this, households keep access to their savings and firms can still pay wages and suppliers, so payments keep flowing.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose is to meet a sudden rush of withdrawals, because a bank keeps only part of its deposits as cash.
Development: the reason is linked to whom it helps - depositors paid, panic contained, and firms and households still able to make payments.

items.prompt: The Bank of Namibia raises its repo rate from 7.0% to 7.5%. Kalahari Furniture of Okahandja has a N$400 000 loan whose interest rate follows the repo rate, and a teacher in the town holds N$20 000 in a savings account. Explain how this central bank decision is likely to affect the firm and the teacher.
items.canonical_answer: The central bank sets the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, and they tend to pass a rise on. A rise of 0.5 percentage points adds about 0.5% of N$400 000 = N$2 000 a year to the firm's interest, so it may delay buying machinery. The teacher's savings earn about 0.5% of N$20 000 = N$100 a year more, though any loan she holds would cost more. Therefore the decision raises borrowing costs for producers and rewards savers.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer uses the figures - the rise from 7.0% to 7.5%, the N$400 000 loan and the N$20 000 of savings.
Reasoning: because commercial banks tend to follow the central bank's rate, loan and savings rates rise with it.
Conclusion: therefore the firm pays about N$2 000 more a year and the teacher earns about N$100 more, which means borrowing is discouraged and saving rewarded.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why a central bank supervises commercial banks.
items.canonical_answer: Commercial banks lend out depositors' money, and a bank that lends too freely or keeps too little in reserve may be unable to repay depositors if many loans go bad. The central bank therefore sets rules on how much each bank must keep in reserve and checks how it lends. Because of this, a bank failure is less likely, so households' savings and firms' funds are safer, and people keep trusting banks enough to deposit with them.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose is to keep deposits safe, because banks lend out depositors' money and may fail if they lend carelessly.
Development: the reason is linked to whom it helps - households and firms whose deposits are protected, and the banking system that depends on their trust.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Money is best defined as:
A  anything that people generally accept as payment for goods and services
B  the notes and coins a government prints
C  the wealth held by households
D  the income earned from work

2. Which of these is a function of money?
A  durability
B  medium of exchange
C  scarcity
D  portability

3. Which of these is a characteristic of money?
A  unit of account
B  store of value
C  divisibility
D  medium of exchange

4. A trader using barter must find a partner who wants what she offers and offers what she wants. This difficulty is called:
A  the double coincidence of wants
B  the store of value problem
C  the unit of account problem
D  the scarcity of money problem

5. A commercial bank is best described as an institution that:
A  accepts deposits from the public and lends the pooled funds to borrowers
B  issues the country's notes and coins
C  holds the government's account
D  lends to commercial banks when their deposits are withdrawn in a rush

6. Which body serves as banker to the government and to the commercial banks?
A  a commercial bank
B  the central bank
C  a savings club
D  a retailer holding a deposit account

7. Money kept as bank deposits rather than as notes and coins is:
A  not money, because it cannot be seen
B  money in a different form, moved by card or phone
C  a store of value but not a medium of exchange
D  wealth rather than money

8. A garment firm borrows from a commercial bank rather than waiting for its own savings because:
A  the loan bridges the gap between paying its costs and receiving its revenue
B  deposits are unsafe while a firm is expanding
C  barter would settle the purchase more quickly
D  the central bank does not lend to firms
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 A, 2 B, 3 C, 4 A, 5 A, 6 B, 7 B, 8 A.
1. General acceptance as payment is the definition (A); B mistakes one form of money for the whole definition, C confuses money with wealth, which includes assets that are hard to spend, D confuses money with income, a flow of earnings.
2. A medium of exchange is a job money does in exchange (B); A, C and D name qualities money needs - characteristics from the other list.
3. Divisibility is a quality a thing needs before people accept it as money (C); A, B and D name jobs money does - functions from the other list.
4. Barter needs two wants to coincide at once (A); B, C and D attach the names of money's functions to a problem that belongs to barter instead.
5. Taking deposits from the public and lending the pooled funds is the commercial bank's work (A); B, C and D each describe the central bank.
6. The central bank banks with the government and the commercial banks themselves (B); A serves households and firms, C is informal saving outside the banking system, D confuses a bank's customer with the bank.
7. Deposits are money in another form, because acceptance rather than material defines money (B); A judges money by what can be seen, C denies a deposit the functions it performs, D confuses money with wealth.
8. The loan bridges the timing gap between costs paid and revenue received (A); B inverts the safety comparison, C reverses the barter relationship, D is true of the central bank but does not explain why the firm borrows.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and each distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Every distractor traces to a named error: the functions list confused with the characteristics list, one form of money taken for its definition, money confused with wealth or income, the central bank confused with a commercial bank.

items.prompt:
A newspaper report from Oshakati, 2026: "Oshakati Textiles, a garment firm employing 60 workers, plans to add a second production line after its orders grew. Its owner told the newspaper: 'Our own savings cover part of the new machines; the rest we are likely to borrow from our bank.' Across the economy, deposits at commercial banks keep climbing."

Table 1 - commercial banks in the economy
  deposits held at commercial banks: N$85 billion last year, N$92 billion this year
  average lending rate on business loans: 9.0% last year, 10.5% this year
  new business loans: 12 000 last year, 14 400 this year

(a) Calculate the rise in deposits held at commercial banks between the two years. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 the average lending rate and the number of new business loans, both for this year. [2]
(c) Explain why Oshakati Textiles keeps its sales revenue as deposits at a commercial bank rather than as notes and coins in a safe. [4]
(d) Analyse, using the data, what the figures suggest about the importance of commercial banks to producers in this economy. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Deposits rose by N$7 billion: 92 - 85 = 7.
(b) The average lending rate is 10.5% and the number of new business loans is 14 400.
(c) Notes in a safe can be stolen, and a safe pays no return, whereas a deposit at a commercial bank is recorded and guarded and usually earns some interest while the bank lends the funds on. Because the firm's customers and suppliers use transfers, the takings arrive as deposits already: holding them as notes would mean withdrawing cash only to bank it again before paying suppliers. Deposits are money in a different form, so the firm loses nothing by keeping its revenue there - the bank can move the money to a supplier's account at once, over any distance, which notes cannot do without travelling. Therefore the firm keeps its revenue as deposits because the account protects the money, links it to the payment system, and lets it earn while it waits.
(d) Where deposits at commercial banks grow, the funds banks can lend to businesses tend to grow with them, and the data fit that pattern: deposits rose from N$85 billion to N$92 billion, and new business loans rose from 12 000 to 14 400, a rise of one fifth, so lending moved with deposits. Producers depend on banks to pool many small deposits into loans large enough to buy machines, as Oshakati Textiles plans to do; the growing number of business loans suggests producers are financing expansion through the banks, and the wages that expansion pays reach households and local shops as spending. The lending rate rising from 9.0% to 10.5% works the other way: borrowing costs more, so some producers may postpone expansion. However, a producer financing machines from its own retained earnings may need no bank at all, and deposits might grow while banks prefer safer assets to business loans, so the trend in deposits is not proof on its own. Producers gain the loans, workers gain the jobs the expansion creates, and the economy gains the output.
marking_guidance: Context: parts (a) and (b) are read straight from the data; part (d) must use the figures as evidence - the deposits, the loan numbers, the lending rate.
Reasoning: one mark per distinct linked statement in (c); a bank service named without the link to the firm earns little.

Conclusion: part (d) runs expected relationship, supporting evidence from the data, analysis, and an exception; quoting figures alone is not analysis - each figure must carry the relationship it supports.

facts: deposits N$85 billion then N$92 billion

items.prompt:
A lodge near Etosha employs 45 workers in peak season and banks with a commercial bank in Windhoek.
(a) Define money. [2]
(b) The lodge quotes its rooms at N$1 200 a night, counts the cost of providing a night at N$450, and reads its bank statement in the same units. Explain how money acting as a unit of account helps the lodge. [4]
(c) Analyse the role commercial banks play for producers and consumers in an economy. [6]
(d) Discuss whether an economy could run its payments system effectively without a central bank. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Money is anything that people generally accept as payment for goods and services and for settling debts; its forms include coins, notes and bank deposits.
(b) A unit of account measures value in one common unit, so the lodge's N$1 200 price means the same number to potential guests wherever they bank. Because price and cost share the unit, the lodge can set the N$1 200 against its N$450 cost and see a difference of N$750 a night, which guides its pricing and how many rooms it offers. Comparisons over time and between suppliers become possible too: when fuel or food prices move, the lodge can track what a night costs it in the same units as its revenue. Therefore the unit of account helps the lodge by making price, cost and the difference between them comparable in one measure.
(c) Producers pay wages and buy materials before their output sells, and consumers need somewhere to keep money between receiving and spending it. A commercial bank accepts deposits from many households and lends the pooled funds to firms, so a producer can borrow for equipment from savers who could not each finance it alone; this causes investment that raises what the firm can produce. Producers gain loans that bridge the gap between paying costs and receiving revenue, and accounts that move payments to suppliers at a distance. Consumers gain deposits that are guarded and usually earn a return, payments that travel without cash, and shelves kept stocked by the firms the loans finance. Workers gain through the jobs the financed expansion supports, and the economy gains the output. However, where a producer has retained earnings of its own it may need no bank, and where savers distrust banks they may hold cash instead, which shrinks the pool banks can lend.
(d) Why it might: most payments already travel between accounts at commercial banks, which settle with one another every day; in principle the banks could keep moving deposits without a central institution, and some countries ran currencies issued by several competing banks in earlier times. Why it might not: the notes and coins households trust need a single issuer behind them, the government needs one account for its taxes and salaries, and when deposits are withdrawn in a rush the commercial banks have no lender of last resort, so one bank's trouble may spread to others and freeze the payments producers and consumers rely on. Judgement: an economy might keep payments moving without a central bank in calm conditions, but the system is likely to be more fragile; the condition the judgement depends on is whether trust in the currency and in deposits holds, and whether the commercial banks can settle with one another when one of them is in trouble.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) to (d) carry a model answer each; (d) is level-marked over three bands, with the top band examining why it might and why it might not and reaching a judgement.
Context: (b) must use the figures - the N$1 200 price and the N$450 cost; (c) must attribute each role to the party it helps - producers, consumers, workers, the economy.
Reasoning: (c) one mark per distinct linked statement; a bank service named without its consequence earns little.
Conclusion: (d) the judgement must name the condition it depends on - whether trust in the currency and in deposits holds.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "The work commercial banks do matters more to an economy than the work the central bank does." Discuss. Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (commercial banks matter more): they carry the economy's daily life - the deposits, loans and payments that producers and consumers touch each week.
Chain 1: savers deposit small sums -> the bank pools them into a loan -> a producer buys machines and pays wages -> output and jobs rise and goods reach consumers, priced in the money whose unit of account lets each deal be measured (for producers, workers, consumers, the economy).
Case against (the central bank matters more): the currency itself and the system's safety come from the central bank, and without them the commercial banks' work has no base to stand on.
Chain 2: deposits are withdrawn in a rush at one bank -> with no lender of last resort it sells assets cheaply -> other banks weaken and payments freeze -> producers cannot pay suppliers and consumers cannot draw money (for firms, households, the whole economy).
Second point for: in ordinary times the central bank is far from most people's daily transactions, whereas a producer or consumer meets a commercial bank every week, so the volume of useful work done is on the commercial side.
Judgement: which bank matters more depends on the condition of the banking system. In calm conditions the commercial banks carry more of the economy's useful daily work; in a crisis the central bank is decisive, because it holds the system together when trust fails. The condition the judgement depends on is whether deposits and the currency are trusted and stable - where they are, commercial banks dominate daily life; where they are not, the central bank matters more.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the case for, the case against, the chains and the judgement are what is assessed.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the condition of the banking system - calm conditions against crisis.
Counterargument: the case for commercial banks must appear as chains, not just the central bank's case.
Condition: the plan must end on what would change the judgement - whether trust in deposits and the currency holds.
